study_identification_part.si4_title: Using normative modelling to detect disease progression in mild cognitive impairment and Alzheimer's disease in a cross-sectional multi-cohort study

study_characteristics_part.sc1_study_objective: This study assessed normative models based on deep autoencoders to detect and quantify deviation from healthy brain patterns in patients with Alzheimer's disease and mild cognitive impairment, and to identify brain regions associated with these deviations.

caa6_deviation_metric.answer: Mean squared error (MSE) between autoencoder reconstruction and input data; Region-specific deviations quantified by Cliff's delta effect size
caa6_deviation_metric.reason: The paper uses two deviation metrics: (1) Overall deviation measured by MSE between reconstruction and input across 101 regions, and (2) Region-specific deviations measured by the difference between input and reconstruction for each region, with effect sizes calculated using Cliff's delta.
caa6_deviation_metric.supporting_text: We calculated the mean squared error between the reconstruction and the inputted data as the metric of brain deviation (Eq. 1). ... The autoencoder approach can quantify how much each brain region deviated from normality and contributed to the observed deviation. These values were obtained by measuring the difference between the inputted value and its reconstruction. ... Then, in each iteration of the bootstrap method, we calculated the effect size of each brain region deviation-using Cliff's delta value-between the HC group and each patient group.

clinical_application_and_analysis_part.caa7_association_analysis: Discriminative performance was assessed using area under the receiver operating characteristic curve (AUC-ROC) for binary classification between healthy controls and patient groups. Group differences in mean deviation scores were tested by examining whether 95% confidence intervals of the difference between groups included zero. Region-specific deviations were compared between HC and patient groups using Mann-Whitney U tests with Cliff's delta effect sizes.
clinical_application_and_analysis_part.caa8_key_findings_brief: The autoencoder-based normative model successfully detected deviations that reflected disease severity (AD > MCI, LMCI > EMCI), with key deviations in medial temporal regions (hippocampus, entorhinal cortex, parahippocampal cortex, amygdala) and ventricular system; performance was comparable to traditional classifiers in most cases.
clinical_application_and_analysis_part.caa9_key_findings_detailed: The normative models generated deviation values that significantly reflected disease severity across five independent datasets. For ADNI, mean deviations were: HC 0.28 [0.27-0.32], EMCI 0.29 [0.28-0.35], LMCI 0.32 [0.30-0.38], AD 0.37 [0.34-0.47]. Similar progressive patterns were observed in AIBL (HC 0.30, MCI 0.36, AD 0.40), ARWiBo (HC 0.32, MCI 0.37, AD 0.46), OASIS-1 (HC 0.41, AD 0.65), and MIRIAD (HC 0.26, AD 0.48). Discriminative performance (AUC) for AD vs HC ranged from 0.75-0.86 across datasets, and for MCI vs HC ranged from 0.60-0.72. Brain regions showing highest deviations in AD included lateral ventricles, temporal horns, hippocampus, entorhinal cortex, parahippocampal cortex, and amygdala. MCI groups showed smaller but overlapping deviations in hippocampus, parahippocampal cortex, and temporoparietal regions. When compared to traditional RVM classifiers, the normative approach showed comparable performance in most cases, with classifiers performing significantly better only for ADNI dataset and AIBL AD predictions. Cross-cohort generalization was comparable between approaches, with no significant differences for MCI prediction.
clinical_application_and_analysis_part.caa11_application_notes: The authors made all scripts and trained models publicly available at https://github.com/Warvito/Normative-modelling-using-deep-autoencoders to promote open science. A Google Colaboratory notebook for calculating deviation scores on new data is also available. The normative approach does not require balanced HC and patient groups for training and can be applied to various clinical tasks (diagnosis, prognosis, treatment selection, mechanistic inference) without retraining. The approach can work cooperatively with conventional discriminative models to identify out-of-distribution examples where supervised methods might fail. The use of large healthy cohorts like UK Biobank (>11,000 participants) enables robust normative modeling without the need for case-control balancing.

caa10_key_limitations.answer: The study did not assess the impact of MRI scanners and acquisition parameters across different datasets. Scanner and acquisition parameter differences may impact model performance, highlighting the need for inter-scanner harmonization methods like Neuroharmony or ComBat. The MCI groups may include heterogeneous cases (both AD and non-AD) since patients were not selected based on AD biomarkers (amyloid-beta and tau), potentially diluting the observed effects. The study used only structural MRI data; multimodal imaging might provide additional information. The UK Biobank training data came from a single scanner site, which may limit generalizability to other scanner types and protocols.

general_note_part.gn1_general_notes: This study represents one of the first applications of deep autoencoder-based normative modeling to neurodegenerative disorders, specifically Alzheimer's disease and MCI. The bootstrapping approach (1,000 iterations) was used extensively to assess robustness and generate confidence intervals for all analyses. The study design involved training on one large dataset (UK Biobank, n=11,034) and validating on five independent clinical datasets (ADNI, AIBL, ARWiBo, OASIS-1, MIRIAD), demonstrating good cross-cohort generalizability. The age range was restricted to 47-73 years across all datasets to ensure consistency. The adversarial autoencoder architecture included: encoder with 2 hidden layers (100 neurons each), latent code (20 neurons), decoder and discriminator with similar structure (2 hidden layers, 100 neurons each), leaky ReLU activation in hidden layers, and linear activation in latent code and decoder output. Training used Adam optimizer with cyclical learning rate (base 0.0001, max 0.005) for 200 epochs with batch size 256. The conditioning approach using one-hot encoding for age (27 positions for ages 47-73) and sex (2 positions) allowed the model to account for these demographic factors in reconstruction. For comparison with traditional machine learning, relevance vector machines (RVM) with linear kernel were used with 0.632+ bootstrap method (1,000 iterations). The complete list of 101 brain regions is provided in supplementary materials.
